context.line: To select the $\langle W, I\rangle$ format (Section~\ref{subsubsec:ponto-fixo}), the BCD-MMSE algorithm was simulated using both fixed-point and 64-bit floating-point matrix inversion. Only the inversion of $\mathbf G_c$ differs between the two simulations; however, the SNR and SER are measured for the entire uplink. Each format was evaluated based on the SNR increase, that is, the additional SNR required by the uplink to achieve an $\mathrm{SER} = 10^{-2}$ compared to the floating-point case. This increase corresponds to the horizontal distance between the two SER curves, which is the standard method for comparing two schemes \cite[p.~55]{tse-viswanath}. The increase is rounded to two decimal places.
after: Two thresholds were employed. A 0.1~dB threshold represents a near-ideal format, where the SER curve is virtually identical to that of the floating-point implementation. A 3~dB threshold serves as the maximum acceptable increase. An increase of 3~dB is equivalent to doubling the power \cite[p.~73]{tse-viswanath}. Consequently, at this threshold, each UE would need to transmit with twice the energy per symbol to compensate for the error introduced by the matrix inversion (Section~\ref{subsec:snr}).

With a limited number of bits, the rounding error in matrix inversion increases with the condition number \cite[p.~1603]{osinsky2023}. The Python simulator runs two nested loops (Figure~\ref{fig:fluxo_python}). The outer loop iterates through the 100 realizations, while the inner loop iterates through the SNR points. The SNR points range from $-10$ to $10$~dB, with a step of $2$~dB. These points form the SNR grid. With QPSK, the grid starts at $-20$~dB, because at $-10$~dB several curves are already at $\mathrm{SER} \leq 10^{-2}$, the point used to compare the equalizers and the formats (Section~\ref{subsec:aumento-snr}). For each realization, the simulator takes $\mathbf{H}$ and $\overline{\mathbf{H}}$ corresponding to that realization and uses these channels across all SNR points. Each point on the SER curves represents the average over the 100 realizations. This is a Monte Carlo simulation, as in \cite{zhuang2025}: the SER (Section~\ref{subsubsec:ser}) is estimated by the fraction of erroneous symbols across many random draws of the channel, noise, and symbols.
context.line: At each SNR point, the simulator constructs the noise covariance matrix based on $\overline{\mathbf{H}}$, the IoTh (interference-over-thermal), and the SNR. It then generates $N$ noise samples, $\mathbf{n}^i$ (Section~\ref{subsubsec:estimacao-R}). It also generates 480 data symbols for each UE, along with the noise associated with these symbols. Based on this, the equalizers are calculated. The channel remains constant within the coherence block (Section~\ref{subsec:bloco-coerencia}); therefore, each equalizer is computed once and applied to all 480 symbols. The BCD-MMSE is compared against two centralized equalizers, the LMMSE and the ZF, which serve as benchmarks. The ZF does not utilize the noise samples $\mathbf{n}^i$. In contrast, both the LMMSE and the BCD-MMSE employ these samples to estimate the noise covariance (Section~\ref{subsubsec:condicionamento-R}). This estimate is always subjected to Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage (Section~\ref{subsubsec:condicionamento-R}) before being used, even in cases where the estimate is already invertible.
after: In the LMMSE, this adjustment is applied to the estimate $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ corresponding to all $M$ antennas. In the BCD-MMSE, each DU performs the adjustment on its own block, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{cc}$, using only the samples from its $M_c$ antennas. Consequently, no DU requires access to the samples from any other DU. The adjusted block forms the matrix $\mathbf{G}_c$ (Section~\ref{subsec:bcd}). In the reference version of the BCD-MMSE, this matrix is inverted using 64-bit floating-point arithmetic; alternatively, it can be inverted using fixed-point arithmetic (Section~\ref{subsubsec:simul-inversa}).

In fixed-point arithmetic, however, some QPSK curves begin with a plateau: a flat, horizontal segment at the top of the plot, corresponding to an SER of 0.75. An SER of 0.75 implies that 3 out of every 4 symbols are incorrect, equivalent to a random selection among the 4 constellation points. Within this plateau, increasing the SNR does not improve the SER; beyond it, the curve drops sharply.

With a greater number of integer bits, the plateau ends at a lower SNR. In groups 1 and 2, the 0.1~dB format differs from the 3~dB format only by having more fractional bits, and the plateau ends at the same SNR. In group 3, the $\langle 30,14\rangle$ format has two more integer bits than the $\langle 24,12\rangle$ format, causing the plateau to end earlier. 16-QAM, on the other hand, operates at higher SNRs and shows almost no variation across the different formats. QPSK is the modulation scheme most sensitive to the number of bits because it operates at lower SNRs, where the elements of $\mathbf G_c$ are larger (Section~\ref{subsec:resultados-grupo2}). When these elements exceed the capacity of the chosen format, an integer overflow occurs, which results in a plateau (Section~\ref{subsubsec:ponto-fixo}). For instance, the $\langle 18,8\rangle$ format can store values up to 128. In the 1C case, the median of the largest element in $\mathbf G_c$ ranges from 70 at $-6$~dB to 164 at $-10$~dB. It exceeds the limit for nearly all matrices at $-10$~dB, while it does not exceed the limit for any matrix at $-6$~dB. It is within this range that the QPSK curve emerges from the plateau. Although the modulation scheme itself does not alter $\mathbf G_c$ (Section~\ref{subsec:hw-matrizes}), 16-QAM operates at higher SNRs, where such overflows occur less frequently.

context.line: Figure~\ref{fig:energia-inversao} shows the energy per inversion, and Table~\ref{tab:energia-inversao} (Appendix~\ref{ap:recursos}) provides the corresponding values. Energy is defined as the dynamic power multiplied by the time required for an inversion (Section~\ref{subsec:hw-potencia}). Consequently, a technique that increases power will only reduce energy if the time per inversion decreases even more significantly. In TDLA30-5, compared to the version without optimizations, the pipelined dividers increase dynamic power by approximately a factor of 5, while the time per inversion decreases by only about a factor of 4. As a result, it consumes more energy than the unoptimized version across all formats. In TDLA30-10, resource utilization remains nearly unchanged relative to TDLA30-5 (Section~\ref{subsec:resultados-recursos}); however, the dataflow reduces the time per inversion, causing the energy to drop by half. When using batches and systolic arrays, the time per inversion decreases at roughly the same rate that power increases, \textcolor{red}{so the four conditions have energies of the same order}. For the $32 \times 32$ case, the unoptimized version utilizes approximately the same amount of resources as the $16 \times 16$ version; however, the time per inversion is longer, leading to an energy consumption approximately 6 times greater than that of the $16 \times 16$ version.
